title_en: Two even maps nested both ways
context_en: Two even maps $p(x)=x^{2} - 1$ and $q(x)=x^{2} + 1$ are nested both ways. Track highest powers, sample values, real roots, and parity of the nestings. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → True

Nesting multiplies highest powers. Each map has degree $2$, so both orders have degree $4$. Expand to confirm nothing cancels.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1$$

$$(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$$

$$p(q(x))=(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1$$

$$(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1=x^{4}+2x^{2}$$

$$2\cdot 2$$

$$(x^{2}+1)^{2}-1=4$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

Each expansion begins with $x^{4}$. Both nested highest powers are $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A nested value is computed inside-out: evaluate $p$ at $0$, then feed that number into $q$.

$$p(0)=-1$$

$$q(p(0))=q(-1)$$

$$q(p(0))=1+1$$

$$q(p(0))=2$$

Expanding $q(p(x))=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$ and substituting $x=0$ gives the same $2$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

The nested value is $2$. Expanding $q(p(x))=x^{4}-2x^{2}+2$ and substituting $x=0$ gives the same $2$. The named value matches.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The other order at the same input is a different composition. Evaluate $q$ at $0$, then feed that number into $p$.

$$q(0)=1$$

$$p(q(0))=p(1)$$

$$p(q(0))=1-1$$

$$p(q(0))=0$$

$$p(q(x))=x^{4}+2x^{2}$$

At $x=0$ that expansion is $0$ as well.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The nested value is $0$. Expanding $p(q(x))=x^{2}(x^{2}+2)$ displays a factor $x^{2}$, which vanishes at the origin. The named value matches.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The outer map $q(u)=u^{2}+1$ is at least $1$ for every real $u$, so composing it with anything never hits height $0$.

$$q(p(x))=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1\ge 1$$

$$(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1\ge 1>0$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

Equivalently $x^{4}-2x^{2}+2=(x^{2}-1)^{2}+1$ has no real root. There is no real root.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

An even inner map makes any outer function of it even, and an even outer map composed with anything even in $x$ is even as well.

$$q(p(-x))=q(p(x))$$

$$p(q(-x))=p(q(x))$$

$$
q(p(-x))=q(p(x))\qquad p(q(-x)) = p(q(x))
$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The composite highest power is the product of the two individual highest powers.

Both expansions contain only even powers. Both nestings are even functions.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview_en:
Both maps are even quadratics.

$$
p(x) = x^{2}-1,\qquad q(x) = x^{2}+1
$$

Nesting multiplies degrees: $2\cdot 2=4$ in either order. Expanding gives different quartics. An even inner map makes any outer function of it even.

$$ $$p(x)=x^{2}-1$$ Die höchste Verbundleistung ist das Produkt der beiden individuellen Höchstleistungen.

Beide Erweiterungen enthalten nur gleichmäßige Kräfte. Beide Nestungen sind sogar Funktionen.

context_en: A cubic is written $p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$. Test distinct zeros, $p'$ at a simple root, parity, Vieta, and the intercept. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements_en: $p$ has exactly three distinct real zeros.
By Vieta, the sum of the three roots is $0$.
tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → True

Three distinct linear factors, each to the first power, give three distinct real zeros.

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$x=-1,\ 1,\ 2$$

$$p(-1)=p(1)$$

$$p(-1)=p(2)$$

$$p(-1)=0$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

None of the factors repeats, so none of the zeros is multiple. The count is three.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A simple root need not flatten the derivative. Differentiate the product and substitute $x=1$.

$$p(x)=(x+1)(x-1)(x-2)$$

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-2x-2$$

$$p'(1)=3-2-2$$

$$p'(1)= -1\neq 0$$

The crossing at $x=1$ is not stationary. The claimed vanishing of $p'$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Oddness requires $p(0)=0$ and $p(-x)=-p(x)$. The intercept is the constant term of the expansion.

$$p(0)=2\neq 0$$

A nonzero intercept already kills oddness.

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

A nonzero intercept kills oddness. The zeros $\{-1,1,2\}$ are not symmetric about the origin either. The cubic is not odd.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Vieta for a monic cubic reads the sum of the roots as minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Add the three simple roots.

$$-1+1=0$$

$$
0+2=2 =2
$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

$$-b=2\neq 0$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$$

Minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient is $-(-2)=2$, not $0$. A vanishing $x^{2}$ term would have been needed for sum $0$. The root sum is $2$, not $0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute $x=0$ into the named polynomial and simplify each power before combining.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - x + 2$$

$$0^{3}=0$$

$$0^{2}=0$$

$$-2\cdot 0=0$$

$$0^{1}=0$$

$$-(0)=0$$

$$p(0)=0+0+0+2$$

$$0+0=0$$

$$0+2=2$$

$$p(0)=2$$

The computed height is $2$, which does not match the claimed $0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview_en:
The cubic is already a product of three distinct monic linear factors.

$$
p(x) = (x-1)(x+1)(x-2) = x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2
$$

Simple roots are crossings, not stationary points. Vieta reads the root sum as minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient. A nonzero intercept kills oddness.

title_en: An odd cubic: factors, Vieta, nesting
context_en: A cubic is given by $p(x)=x \left(x^{2} - 4\right)$. Test parity, the factor theorem, Vieta, nested degree, and the distinct-zero count. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements_en: By Vieta, the multiplicity-weighted sum of real roots of $p$ is $0$.
tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → True

Oddness is the identity $p(-x)=-p(x)$, which holds as soon as only odd powers appear.

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+4x$$

$$-x^{3}+4x=-p(x)$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{3}-4(-x)$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+4x$$

$$p(x)=x(x^{2}-4)$$

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

There is no even-power term and no leftover constant. The cubic is odd.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The factor theorem at $x=2$ is immediate from the given product, or from substituting.

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$p(2)=2\cdot 0\cdot 4$$

$$2\cdot 0=0$$

$$0\cdot 4=0$$

$$p(2)=0$$

$$2\cdot 0\cdot 4$$

$$p(2)=2\cdot 0\cdot 4$$

$$2\cdot 0=0$$

$$p(x)=x(x^{2}-4)$$

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

The factor $x-2$ is visible before any expansion. So $x-2$ divides $p$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Vieta for a monic cubic reads the multiplicity-weighted root sum as minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient. Add the three simple roots.

$$-2+0=-2$$

$$
-2+2=0 =0
$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

$$-b=0$$

$$p(x)=x(x^{2}-4)$$

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

The $x^{2}$ coefficient is already $0$, matching the sum. The multiplicity-weighted root sum is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Nesting multiplies highest powers: substituting $x^{2}$ into a cubic produces degree $3\cdot 2=6$.

$$p(x^{2})=x^{2}((x^{2})^{2}-4)$$

$$x^{2}((x^{2})^{2}-4)=x^{6}-4x^{2}$$

$$p(x)=x(x^{2}-4)$$

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-4x$$

The leading coefficient remains $1$, so the degree does not drop. The nested highest power is $x^{6}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Three distinct linear factors display three distinct real zeros. Write the product and list the roots.

$$p(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$
x=-2,\qquad x = 0,\qquad x = 2
$$

$$p(-2)=p(0)$$

$$p(-2)=p(2)$$

$$p(-2)=0$$

None of the factors repeats, and each substitution confirms a zero. The count is three.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview_en:
The cubic is given as a product, which already displays the three real linear factors.

$$
p(x) = x(x^{2}-4) = x(x-2)(x+2) = x^{3}-4x
$$

Only odd powers appear, so $p$ is odd. Vieta reads the root sum as minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient. Nesting multiplies degrees: substituting $x^{2}$ produces $x^{6}$.

title_en: A double root fixed at the origin
context_en: A monic cubic family is given by $h_{k}(x)=x^{2}(x-k)$. The double root is pinned at the origin; the simple root slides with $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements_en: For every real $k$, $h_{k}$ is an odd function of $x$.
If $k=2$, then $h_{k}$ has exactly two distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → False

Oddness requires only odd powers. Expanding the family shows an $x^{2}$ term as soon as $k\neq 0$.

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx^{2}$$

$$h_{1}(-x)=-x^{3}-x^{2}$$

$$-h_{1}(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{2}(x-k)$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx^{2}$$

That even-power term survives for every $k\neq 0$, so $h_{k}(-x)\neq -h_{k}(x)$ in general. Only the special case $k=0$ gives the odd map $x^{3}$. Oddness fails as soon as $k\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity. For $k=2$ the factors are $x^{2}$ and $x-2$.

$$h_{2}(x)=x^{2}(x-2)$$

$$
x=0,\qquad x = 2
$$

$$
h_{2}(0)=0\qquad h_{2}(2) = 0
$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{2}(x-k)$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx^{2}$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Those are two distinct abscissas: a double root at the origin and a simple root at $2$. Exactly two distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A double root flattens the derivative. For $k=2$ the double root is pinned at the origin, so differentiate and substitute.

$$h_{2}'(x)=3x^{2}-4x$$

$$3x^{2}-4x=x(3x-4)$$

$$h_{2}'(0)=0$$

$$h_{2}'(x)=x(3x-4)$$

The double-root rule forces $h_{2}'(0)=0$.

The claimed inequality is the wrong way around: the derivative does vanish at $0$. The double-root rule applies.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Every member is monic of odd degree, so the right end follows $x^{3}$ upward. For the named parameter,

$$h_{2}(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}$$

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}h_{2}(x)=+\infty$$

$$h_{2}(10)=1000-200$$

$$h_{2}(10)=800>0$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{2}(x-k)$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx^{2}$$

Compare the expanded formula at $-x$ with the negative of the original.

$$p(-x)\stackrel{?}{=}-p(x)$$

The leading term $x^{3}$ is positive for large positive $x$. The right end rises, not falls.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The double factor $x^{2}$ forces every graph through the origin, independently of $k$.

$$h_{2}(0)=0$$

$$h_{k}(0)=0$$

The family never has a leftover constant term.

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{2}(x-k)$$

$$h_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx^{2}$$

The factor test succeeds only when that substitution returns zero.

Read the intercept as the value at the origin.

$$p(0)$$

The intercept is $0$, not $2$. A claimed intercept $2$ would have needed a leftover constant term, which the family never has. The intercept is $0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview_en:
The family keeps a double root at the origin and lets the simple root slide with $k$.

$$
h_{k}(x) = x^{2}(x-k) = x^{3}-kx^{2}
$$

Every member is a monic cubic, so the right end always rises. An $x^{2}$ term destroys oddness as soon as $k\neq 0$. The intercept is $0$ for every $k$.
